subject: chemistry
question_text: What is hydrogen bond? Explain the types of hydrogen bonds with example.

verification.note: Chapter 3 is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.56-61), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. TWO corrections to the book: (1) its definition omits that the hydrogen atom must already be covalently bonded to the electronegative atom; (2) it defines the intermolecular type as 'between two different polar molecules' while its own examples (H₂O, HF, NH₃) are chains of ONE substance — the card says two separate molecules, of the same or of different substances.

steps.label: Definition
lines: Hydrogen bond: the weak electrostatic force
of attraction between a hydrogen atom that
is covalently bonded to a highly
electronegative atom (F, O or N) and
It is weaker than a covalent bond.
steps.why: The H atom gets a partial positive charge only because it is already bonded to F, O or N. That charge is what the second electronegative atom attracts, so both halves of the sentence are needed.
common_mistakes: Writing a bond between hydrogen and any atom. Only F, O and N are electronegative enough.
Calling it a covalent bond. It is a weak electrostatic attraction.
steps.memory_tip: Remember the three letters F, O, N — the only partners electronegative enough.
steps.margin_note: Naming F, O, N in brackets is expected in the definition.

steps.label: The diagram
steps.why: The chain of HF molecules shows exactly which link is the hydrogen bond: the dotted line from the δ⁺ hydrogen of one molecule to the δ⁻ fluorine of the next. The solid lines are ordinary covalent bonds.
common_mistakes: Drawing the hydrogen bond as a solid line. Solid is covalent; the hydrogen bond is the dotted link.
Leaving off the δ⁺ and δ⁻ charges, which are the cause of the attraction.
steps.memory_tip: Solid line inside a molecule, dotted line between molecules.
steps.margin_note: Three H−F units with two dotted links is the standard exam sketch.

steps.label: Intermolecular type
lines: between two separate molecules, of the
same substance or of different substances.
Ex: H₂O, HF and NH₃ — in liquid HF the
steps.why: This is the type in the diagram above: the bond crosses from one molecule to another, which is why it raises boiling points of liquids such as water and HF.
common_mistakes: Writing that the two molecules must be of different substances. Water bonded to water is the standard example.
Giving no example. H₂O or HF is expected.
steps.memory_tip: Inter means between: the bond runs between two separate molecules.
steps.margin_note: Point back to the chain diagram — it is the example drawn out.

steps.label: Intramolecular type

lines.text: Intramolecular hydrogen bond: within one molecule

lines: 2. Formed between the hydrogen atom and an
electronegative atom present in the SAME
steps.why: The contrast with the first type is the point: the same attraction, but both ends sit inside a single molecule, forming a ring within it.
common_mistakes: Swapping the two names: intra is within one molecule, inter is between molecules.
Giving H₂O as the example here. Water's hydrogen bonds are intermolecular.
steps.memory_tip: Intra means inside: both ends of the bond are in one molecule. The two standard examples are the ortho compounds.
steps.margin_note: The two ortho examples are the ones the paper expects by name.

insider_note: Name both types with one example each — and keep the examples on the correct sides: H₂O and HF are INTERmolecular, the two ortho compounds are INTRAmolecular.
